subcategory: Black Hills ponderosa pine forest/prairie native

planting.note: Fall sow onto lean, well-drained granitic or sandy-loam soil in dappled light to full sun, letting winter cold-moist stratification trigger spring germination; this is the dominant understory sedge carpeting the open floor of Black Hills ponderosa pine savanna.

directions: Sun sedge spreads by slender rhizomes to form a low, fine-textured sod beneath the open canopy of Black Hills ponderosa pine stands, where it is often the single most abundant ground-layer plant, tolerating both the dappled shade of mature pines and the fuller sun of thinned or burned openings. It stays green and wiry through drought and resprouts readily after the low-intensity fires that keep ponderosa savanna open, making it a useful groundcover under pines or on dry slopes where turf grass struggles. Give it lean, fast-draining soil and avoid rich, consistently moist beds, which favor coarser weedy competitors over this naturally thin, wind-firm sod. Once established it needs no mowing or supplemental water beyond an occasional dry-spell soak.

subcategory: Black Hills ponderosa pine forest/prairie native

planting.note: Sow fresh seed shallowly in fall on lean, gravelly or clay-loam soil in an open or lightly wooded site; seed needs a full winter of cold, moist stratification and often germinates erratically over more than one season.

directions: Nuttall's violet is one of the earliest wildflowers to bloom on the dry, grassy openings and thin ponderosa pine edges of the Black Hills, sending up stemless clusters of lance-shaped, gray-green leaves and small butter-yellow flowers with faint brownish-purple veining on the lower petals as the snow retreats. Unlike the moist-woodland violets common in eastern gardens, it thrives in lean, rocky or clay-loam soil with excellent drainage and resents summer watering once it has gone dormant after flowering. It is best used in a dry prairie or rock-garden planting rather than a shaded border, and self-sows modestly where happy. Foliage dies back by midsummer heat, so pair it with later-blooming companions that can fill the gap.

subcategory: Black Hills ponderosa pine forest/prairie native

planting.note: Fall sow into well-drained loam in a partly shaded ponderosa-edge or meadow setting; the hard seed coat benefits from a winter outdoors, and nicking or lightly scarifying stored seed speeds germination if sowing in spring instead.

directions: Sticky purple geranium fills the sunny-to-lightly-shaded meadows and ponderosa pine openings of the Black Hills with mounds of deeply lobed, hairy foliage and five-petaled magenta-pink flowers held above the leaves through early-to-midsummer. The common name comes from the noticeably glandular, slightly sticky texture of the stems and sepals, a trait that helps distinguish it from the similar native sticky geraniums found elsewhere in the Rockies. It grows best with a touch more moisture and shade than the fully exposed shortgrass prairie natives it borders, making it a good choice for the transition zone between a dry prairie planting and a pine-shaded bed. Cut plants back by half after the main flush fades to encourage tidier regrowth and occasional rebloom.

subcategory: Black Hills ponderosa pine forest/prairie native

planting.note: Sow onto lean, gritty or gravelly soil in full sun in early spring, pressing seed in lightly; good drainage matters more than soil fertility for this dry-ground native of granite outcrops and pine-savanna openings.

directions: Shaggy fleabane forms a dense, grayish, densely hairy tuft of narrow leaves on the dry granite outcrops and open ponderosa savanna of the Black Hills, sending up a profusion of slender stems tipped with narrow-rayed, lavender-to-white daisies through late spring and summer. Its silvery, shaggy pubescence is a visible adaptation to the intense sun and wind exposure of exposed rock and gravel sites, and the plant performs poorly in rich, shaded, or consistently damp ground. Use it in a dry rock garden, gravel bed, or along a sunny path edge where its low mounding habit and long bloom season can be appreciated up close. Shear spent flowering stems back after the main bloom to keep the clump tidy and encourage a smaller rebloom later in the season.

subcategory: Black Hills ponderosa pine forest/prairie native

planting.note: Surface-sow the fine seed onto lean, well-drained soil in early spring and keep lightly moist until the mat of basal rosettes establishes; it spreads readily afterward by stolons and needs no further coddling.

directions: Rosy pussytoes creeps by wiry stolons into a low, silvery-gray mat of felted basal leaves across the dry, open ground between pines and granite outcrops of the Black Hills, sending up short flowering stems in early summer tipped with clusters of papery, rose-pink-tinged bracted flower heads. The silver foliage and pink-blushed blooms distinguish it from the more purely white-bracted pussytoes species found on the adjacent shortgrass steppe, and it tolerates foot traffic and light grazing in the wild. In the garden it makes a durable, drought-proof groundcover for a sunny gravel path, dry slope, or the gaps between flagstones, spreading steadily without becoming invasive in lean soil. Avoid rich, moist beds, which cause the mat to rot or become overrun by taller neighbors.

subcategory: Black Hills ponderosa pine forest/prairie native

planting.note: Tuck small divisions or nursery plugs into vertical or angled crevices between limestone or granite rocks in spring, packing gritty, lean soil tightly around the short rhizome so the crown sits just below the rock surface.

directions: Fee's lipfern is a diminutive, densely hairy fern that wedges its wiry rhizomes into the cracks of limestone and granite outcrops across the Black Hills and the wider Great Plains and Rocky Mountain foothills, curling its small fronds tightly inward during drought and unfurling again within hours of rain. It is one of the few ferns able to thrive on fully exposed, baking rock faces rather than in shaded, moist woodland soil, making it a specialty choice for a crevice or dry rock garden rather than a conventional fern bed. Plant it where water drains away immediately and never sits around the crown, and resist the urge to treat its shriveled, drought-dormant look as a sign of failure. Established plants are extremely long-lived in the right crevice and need essentially no maintenance beyond occasional removal of fallen leaf litter.
